title: Promises, Not Proofs
subtitle: How a program becomes a hand-wired neural network, told in the things people were sure of
devices: Promise Tags on the copper line over the log-scale Lifespan Rule: front = the belief (paraphrase unless verbatim), knot = who tied it on (empty knot when the bible names no holder), back = the red pencil's dissent; struck once in red when broken, copper rivet when kept or confirmed; signature grommet (stamped = the repo names it, empty = it doesn't) drawn only where the bible settles it (empty on 1943/1951/1990s, stamped on SKLANSKY 1960 and BRENT · KUNG 1982). Eleven tags plus one blank; no sub-tags.
Window Calendar: one lit pane per commit, exact counts (June 72, July 6, August dark with snow on the sill, September 58, October 689 with 683 in four columns); ch03, ch08, ch09, ch12.

X-ray desk: HandwiredOS revealed in ch01; then 4–6 s silent returns at the ends of ch03–ch07, one more real component lit each time (source table, ReGLU ramps and shutters, loom, host ratchet, a dark valve with its one line); plain again in ch12.

Score: the both-branches motif (two lines a whole tone apart always playing, a 0/1 gain gate choosing; both at half level for 4.5, the musical eleven) and the detent figure (tie, flip, strike; the third stroke withheld for beliefs still held, replaced by the gate at 0.5 for the two still contested). Machines clack, never chime.

Spoken refrains: 'Who tied it on. Who doubted it. How long it held.' in full exactly three times (ch01-s07, ch04-s09, ch08-s03), turned in ch12-s06; 'Hang that on the line.' exactly four times (ch01-s05, ch02-s03, ch03-s06, ch05-s06).

chapters.title: Four and a Half
chapters.summary: A copper thread resolves into the wire under HandwiredOS's dock. The desk is revealed early: a window glides and settles, Monitor shows 'State 234 · Operations 4,646 · Outputs 493', and the camera passes through into the wallpaper's 9,909 arcs, one per weight. The narrator ties the viewer's three likely guesses onto the copper line as suspect tags (somebody trained it; a tool turned ordinary code into it; it isn't really a network), two with empty knots: 'Hang them on the line.' Then the README's (a > 4) ? 10 : 12 as two ramps and a lever: five gives ten, three gives twelve, four and a half gives eleven, with both shutters half open and the score's two lines at half level. The tag inks itself with the README's small print 'For an integer a'; the red pencil stops short. First full refrain; title card with the detent figure's third stroke withheld.
chapters.turn: The machine isn't broken. It was built for whole numbers, and it took that on trust.

chapters.title: The Oldest Tags
chapters.summary: Framing only, captioned 'context: the repo cites none of this work' [FR22]. A 1943 Chicago study: McCulloch and Pitts tie on tag 1 (the neuron is a logic gate), its signature grommet empty; Q133 read. Paper lanterns compute AND and OR, and nothing in them learns (planted for DD III); von Neumann's EDVAC report borrows the idea. 1951: Kleene finds part of it 'obscure', keeps the model, and proves such a net is a finite machine stepping once per tick; the patterns it recognises are regular events; 'Anything unbounded, like time itself, has to come from outside. Hang that on the line.' 1959's frog (the same two men; reading it as refutation came later) and 2020's graded dendritic spikes split tag 1's thread: as biology it frays at about sixteen years, as engineering it runs off the rule glowing. Tag 2: Sutton's bitter lesson against Brooks, dominant not consensus. The log-scale Lifespan Rule explained once for the ear. 'Eighty-three years later, someone wrote a network's weights by hand again. Not from that paper.'
chapters.turn: Into that world comes a project that writes its weights by hand.

chapters.title: Deep Dive I: Promises, Not Proofs
chapters.summary: The README's (a > 4) ? 10 : 12 worked by hand on one growing machine. In JavaScript only the chosen arm runs. A bit of the copper line bends into a ReLU hinge and grows into the first ramp, max(0, a − 4), read at 3, 4, 5, 6, 100; the second ramp one step later; the lever's difference, clamp(a − 4, 0, 1), with whole numbers on its corners. Both belts always run and a 0/1 shutter picks; an infinity on the closed belt still poisons the tray to NaN. Four and a half gives 11 (4.25 gives 11.5); past 2^24, 16,777,222 gives 8. What the runtime builds: emitCompare demands a declared range, so tag 6 is re-tied onto the wire of a as 'grid 1' and the comparison shrinks to 2 operations (whole ternary 8 in 5 layers). Pushed to 4.5 under the grid tag it says 11 and the validator objects: Q029, 'Declarations are promises from the caller, not proofs.', the chapter's climax and the second full refrain. With no promise, the lens train magnifies by 2^149 in 16 operations and answers 10. One honest sentence saves fourteen operations. The 8,388,609 detent paid. What exact means (Q036; the 1,732 px window); why not doubles (18,820 of 20,000 labels wrong); a wall of 4,402 checks. Q038 planted silently. X-ray: ReGLU ramps and shutters light.
chapters.turn: Every if here is a dimmer switch. The program's whole job is to keep it fully on, or fully off.

chapters.title: One Big Matmul
chapters.summary: The builder ribbon feeds the matmul loom: 130 thin frames by dependency depth (Q039), copper threads adding and indigo subtracting, mostly empty air. Sheets of sums fuse and stop dead at a gate frame (longest gate chain 71); Q006, 'a giant matmul'. Suspect tag 5 struck: it is a network in the plain sense, layers of weighted sums with ReLU gates (PR04). The camera exits the loom to find its threads are the wallpaper: 4,646 live operations · 130 layers · 9,909 weights; the site's build fails if those drift. The Notes plant paid: on 13 October, when Notes handed its text back to the browser's text box, the loom shed most of its threads, 19,851 → 4,251 operations. The cold furnace: everything runs as JavaScript on the CPU (Q041); an older 14,019-operation build on WebGPU, one machine, 16 September, ran about twenty-seven times slower and its 6.4 MB shader had not compiled in 28 minutes. 'So what is a GPU for? Hang that on the line.' X-ray: the loom lights.
chapters.turn: So what is a GPU for?

chapters.title: Deep Dive II: The Clockwork That Cannot Stop
chapters.years: the host loop, springs and patterns
chapters.summary: Q015 is the thesis: a program can't stop early, so a loop becomes a count, a tree, a table, or the same work on every item, and the four nouns become the four arms of a host clockwork. One turn: the toggle's handler only queues a timestamped token (Q026); at the frame the host writes inputs and four matrix cards into the pigeonholes, the loom runs once, next-state cards are copied back, the page moves from outputs, and the clock stops when nothing moves (Q027). Springs without loops: a brass 2×2 stamp turns −300, 0 into −298.608, 348; a squaring press folds 300 steps into 8 squarings while the program pays 14 operations in 3 layers for any step count. The 300-tooth ratchet snaps (snap versus carry is a design choice). Two desks at 10 and 120 fps: 359 px apart in the familiar order, identical in every bit in Handwired's, in the repo's tests; tag 7 (one evaluation per frame) struck at 15 September. The four arms: a count (findIndex as the counting rail, 3); a tree (the prefix loom with paper name tags SKLANSKY 1960 and BRENT · KUNG 1982, signed into the runtime as function names; Brent's 'unpopular'; 799.300048828125 vs 799.2999877929688; the CPU loop faster, the tree more accurate at 10,000 rows); a table (30,002 operations as arithmetic vs 1 index read); the same work on every item (ranks 2 0 3 1 with no swaps; the K-slot rack and Monitor's 'Only 64 rows are drawn at a time.'). Kleene paid: the network is one fixed, exact step and the host loop turns the crank (one card each for Siegelmann & Sontag and Maass & Orponen; Q127). X-ray: the ratchet lights.
chapters.turn: The network is one fixed, exact step. The host loop turns the crank. It never stops early.

chapters.title: Deep Dive III: Unfreezing
chapters.summary: The README's offer, Q010 (planted for the epilogue): a frozen weight-knob cracks its ice. One ReGLU valve by hand: w = 0.5, g = 0.25, b = −0.1 opens to 0.15 and outputs 0.225; backward, slopes 0.45 and 1.5. Lower b to −0.4 and the valve shuts: output 0, every gradient 0 (Q108); a whisper of decay keeps gates alive; ch02 paid: 'McCulloch and Pitts's neurons couldn't learn. These can, if you let them.' Backward rules run on the loom (Q052). Tag 10, 'fully differentiable', doubted from inside the repo: DD I's ramps are flat at every whole number (Q110); it stays hanging. The learned gallery on a misty-hills stage: 244 weights, 6,320 operations in 8 layers, photos piled as small squares; a clerk with a seating chart (plain JavaScript decides who, the network learns where); the Huber clamp caps each pull at 0.08 (far-off photos vote, they don't shout), the bias gradient formula, Adam's first step 0.5 → ≈0.492; photos fan out at 600 steps a second. The snapping shortcut refused (Q106, Q107). Honest scope: a small generic network compiled, not a hand-written one unfrozen; true unfreezing in drag-knobs solved 63.6% of drag frames in one step; the nanoGPT dream (Q011) hangs as a question tag, not attempted. X-ray: a dark valve, 'Not one of its weights is trained.'
chapters.turn: The desktop has none of this switched on. Not one of its weights is trained.

chapters.title: The Summer's Certainties
chapters.summary: The Window Calendar dims: six panes in July, and August entirely dark with snow on the sill ('The record doesn't say why. So we won't guess.'). Lab round one lands four experiments on 8 July, and tag 8, 'established conclusions: take these as given' (a label), is tied on by the July briefs from an unnamed design conversation, not Cheng. At 06:13 on 3 September, a grey dawn: the reassessment, an AI agent's review by its own account, writes ten short red strokes on the tag's back, over the third and last full refrain. Three of them on plates: a 0/20 learning result became 20/20 when every loss was multiplied by a million (a tiny optimiser constant), with its own caution that this doesn't show the method scales; the checker that shared the bug (JavaScript 3, compiled 4, zero mismatches; Q116), with DD I's Q038 plate sliding back in beside it; the gradient of 3v at zero, 0 or 3 by operand order. Fixed that morning, 274 tests passing; Q118 names the danger. The film's one plain sentence about tooling, over the two hands at one keyboard: 825 commits authored by Cheng Lou, 756 crediting Claude Code, an earlier Codex discussion, and this film written with Claude; a process, not a scorecard. 14–15 September: the recommended option chosen each time; September's 58 panes relight; tag 8 hangs struck, about eight weeks.
chapters.turn: Mistakes made with agents were found by reviews run with agents, under his direction.

chapters.title: Four Days in October
chapters.summary: The Window Calendar blazes: October's 689 panes, 683 crowded into four columns for 13 to 16 October, lit in every hour. Two lamplit cards in Cheng's own lowercase: his GPU question (Q099 substring) and 'Maybe we should check before we build it.' (Q100 substring), the film's temperament in seven words. JSON search gets its own machine time: a map of 100,000 tiny cells, one document each, one GPU thread per document running the same small step; the GPU plant paid with Q090 (it is for many documents). Match cut: Kleene's typed RAND page becomes the search pattern written as cells, 'a new pattern writes cells and changes no program' (Q096): regular events, seventy-five years on, read by a hundred thousand threads, with the honest caption that the repo cites Thompson and Cox, not Kleene. Two clerks walk each strip backward then forward, because a program can't go back. The RegExp booth with its ten-second hourglass: 11–15 ms a keystroke against 8–28, and 2.1 seconds against about 11 ms on a backtracking pattern, one machine. Tag 9, 'the GPU is the faster one', tied at 09:01 and struck by a review within hours, the shortest thread in the film; Q092, Q095. The go-ahead in a commit (Q103), the repo public on the evening of 14 October, the launch post (Q104 substring).

chapters.title: Strangers with Pencils
chapters.summary: Reception as text cards over a dusk sky; Hacker News commenters are never drawn. A Show HN on 20 October; the critic's 'DSL' line (Q130) reaches tag 4 and finds the strike already there in the repo's own hand (Q014), with the fair note that another reader read it as a compiler. The 4.5 → 11 finding (Q131), nine days after the repo went public: tag 6 flips, and its back already carried the landing page's hidden comment about the 11 and the 8; the rivet holds, a promise that states its limits is kept. 'why?' (Q132) is hung on the line as a question tag for the epilogue. No public discussion of the lab was found: the strangers' pencils were gentler than the lab's own.

TOML: Q123, its half struck by its own pre-set rule, then scoped honestly by Q124. The bison track's final test not run: an open loop. The ledger's Still open drawer slides out with Q125 and stays open.

chapters.title: One More Neuron
chapters.summary: Out through a window bay onto misty hills at dawn: the copper line strung across the valley with all eleven tags at their lifespans, the Window Calendar dark after 16 October in the distance. The narrator's hands re-hang every tag one column to the right of the deepest tag you needed to understand it (the compiler's own rule, applied to the film's teaching order, computed not placed), and the washing line becomes a loom. A forward wave of copper light runs through every column; struck tags light too and are multiplied by zero ('The struck ones ran too. Multiplied by zero.'). Tags 2 and 10 glow off the rule, undecided (the score's two lines at half level); the 'why?' tag is answered by the README's own Q010. Back at the plain desk, Notes' last line: 'Wire one more neuron by hand'. The narrator bends a copper hinge, ties the blank tag to it and places it in the viewer's open hand: 'Who tied it on, we know. Who will doubt it, we don't. It's waiting for the next pair of hands.' The wire under the dock is the last light; end card: as of 27 October 2026, main is still at 257856e.
chapters.turn: It's waiting for the next pair of hands.
